figures.caption: Table 4: Main hidden-test performance and reward decomposition by core regime (N=480 episodes each). E2E Q counts missing terminal hidden-test scores as zero, Obs. Q averages only scored episodes. Rperf , Rplan, Rcode are the mean contributions of the performance, plan-coverage, and code-quality terms to the final reward R. Higher is better throughout. This table supports H1, H2, H4, and H5.
Table 18: Harness regimes evaluated in GRACE-DS.

Table 19: Operating times by regime (per-episode means, all 15 regimes evaluated in the grid). Median time is reported with its inter-quartile range [Q1, Q3] because the per-episode wall-clock is long-tailed. Tokens are in thousands. The last column reports the seconds-per-unit-of-quality ratio t̄sec/E2E Q as a single-number efficiency summary (lower is better). The red_team_vs_validators row uses the matched red-team scope (N=120), all other rows use the core scope (N=480).

Table 20: Operating times per model under flexible_iterative (60 episodes per model). The single-shot mean wall-clock is shown for comparison to make the iteration overhead per model explicit. Models are sorted by the seconds-per-unit-of-quality ratio under flexible iteration (lower is better).

Table 11: Runtime, iteration, and budget-use statistics by core regime (means per episode, Valid. is the number of evaluator-scored validations, Val. delta is the mean within-episode improvement of the gated validation metric on the normalized scale, with the fraction of validated episodes that improved in parentheses). This table supports H2 and H9.

Figure 2: Model× regime structure of end-to-end quality. Each cell is colored by the mean end-to-end normalized hidden-test quality (E2E Q) of the corresponding model and regime (multiply the test score by the coverage), the cell annotation reports the mean observed quality on scored episodes together with the scored-episode coverage out of the 60 episodes per cell (10 tasks × 6 repeats). Reading across a row isolates the effect of the harness regime at fixed model capability: every model attains its highest E2E Q under the structured in-environment regimes, and the column for flexible_iterative is uniformly the strongest. This figure is the per-cell view behind the model-level aggregates in Table 10.

Figure 1: GRACE-DS evaluates LLM AutoML agents in a staged tabular environment. The evaluator owns the split and the private valid/hidden-test labels (top row). The agent (bottom row) sees only training labels and validation features and iterates LLM agent → restricted execution → reproducible candidate. Each candidate is gated by validation, and the agent receives only abstract stage and metric feedback. Scoring is evaluator-owned: every candidate is run through evaluator-side replay (dashed red), and the selected one yields a single hidden-test score.

Figure 4: End-to-end quality across the autonomy spectrum for three representative models. Mean E2E Q for GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-5.4, and Qwen3.5-397b-a17b under three regimes of increasing structure: independent restarts from scratch, the unstructured agent, and flexible structured iteration.

Figure 3: Model× regime rate of any risky behavior. A run is counted as risky if it exhibits at least one execution error, critical methodological error, protocol violation, forbidden-action attempt, or payload error, cells are colored by the per-cell rate and annotated with the number of risky episodes out of 60. The single-shot and restart columns concentrate the leakage-class critical errors, whereas the structured-feedback columns (fixed_stage_iterative, flexible_compact_feedback, flexible_iterative) are near-zero, consistent with the aggregate error and recovery statistics in Table 6.

Table 9: Leave-one-state-out ablations. Mean columns report each regime directly, delta columns report the ablation minus its full counterpart (paired, 480 pairs, † marks Wilcoxon p < 0.01). Negative ∆E2E Q indicates the removed state was load-bearing. This table supports H7.

Table 10: Model-level breakdown (mean E2E Q per model under selected regimes, 60 episodes per model-regime cell). ∆Flex-SS is flexible_iterative minus single_shot, ∆Flex-CM is flexible_iterative minus callmatched restarts. Fixed PV is protocol validity under the prescribed schedule, illustrating the scale-dependent collapse discussed in the text. This table supports H8 and H9.

Table 14: Mapping of the hypotheses to the experiments and the output tables that operationalize them, serving as a roadmap for the experiments described in the rest of this section. Regime names are those of Table 18, the primary output names are the aggregated CSV tables defined in the “Budgets and replication” paragraph below. H8 and H10 are read as per-model and per-task breakdowns of those tables, H9 additionally has a dedicated quality-speed-cost table.

Figure 5: Regime-level relationship between the mean final process reward and the mean observed normalized hidden-test quality, one point per regime. At the regime level the two move together, but this aggregate trend should not be read as an episode-level alignment guarantee: as discussed in Section 5.4, the reward-quality correlation must be assessed per task and per cell, and the reward-maximization probes in Table 7 show that reward can be raised slightly while end-to-end quality falls. This figure supports the reward-alignment analysis of Section 5.4.

Table 8: Red-team stress test against the validators. “Defended” counts model-task rows with no uncaught reward advantage in the validator-defense analysis, which spans 4 models × 10 tasks. The per-episode rows (Episodes, E2E Q, Obs. Q, R, PV, the error and violation counts, and the paired deltas) report the matched two-model headto-head (GPT-5.4 and Qwen3.5-397B, N=120 episodes per column), whereas the Defended model-task rows and Mean uncaught reward advantage rows summarize that 4 models × 10 tasks grid. The adversary achieves no critical error, no evaluator-private access, no snapshot tampering, and no forbidden-action attempt, and loses both reward and hidden-test quality. This table supports H3, H4, and H6.
Table 16: GRACE-DS configuration values used in the paper grid. Reward weights and the penalty cap also appear in Eqs. (1)–(3), they are listed here for a single point of reference.

Table 6: Error and recovery statistics by core regime. “Any error” is episode-level and includes execution errors, critical errors, protocol violations, forbidden-action attempts, and terminal payload errors. Critical errors (all leakage variants here) force the episode reward to zero. Recovery is the fraction of error episodes that still end protocol-valid. This table supports H3 and H4.
Table 21: Summary of hypothesis outcomes with the primary supporting evidence.

Figure 6: Quality-cost frontier by regime. Mean output-token consumption per episode (horizontal axis) against end-to-end normalized hidden-test quality (vertical axis), one marker per regime, the structured in-environment regimes are drawn as stars, with the flexible regimes distinguished from the fixed schedule. Flexible iteration sits at the top of the quality axis while spending fewer tokens than the call-matched restart upper bound, and the compact-feedback variant trades a small quality decrement for a reduced token budget. This figure complements the wall-clock and efficiency analysis of Section 5.8 and Table 11.

Table 3: The eight LLMs in the GRACE-DS paper grid. All are open-weight except the three marked prop. (proprietary) (gemini-3.1-pro, grok-4.3, gpt-5.4), whose architectures are undisclosed. MoE=mixture-ofexperts (total/active parameters where disclosed), reasoning is enabled where supported.

Table 1: States (action vocabulary) of the GRACE-DS environment. “Exec.” marks states that run a fenced Python block, VALIDATE/FINAL_SUBMIT are evaluator triggers. The per-state step, time and repeat budgets are listed in Table 15.

Table 12: Task-level breakdown (mean E2E Q per task, 48 episodes per task-regime cell), sorted by the improvement of flexible_iterative over single_shot. This table supports H10 and shows where iterative modeling gives the largest gains.
